gateway.description:
Gateway API configuration, consumed by `common.gateway.*`. The successor to `ingress`, and
an independent switch from it: a cluster migrating between an Ingress controller and a Gateway
implementation runs both for a while.

The division of labour is the API's, not this chart's. A `Gateway` — the listeners, the
address, the certificates — belongs to the cluster operator; an application owns only the
`HTTPRoute` that attaches to it. So the default here is route-only, and `create` is for
installs that have no cluster-wide Gateway to attach to.

addresses.description: Addresses requested for the created Gateway, e.g. a fixed `IPAddress`.
addresses.title: addresses

allowedRoutes.description:
Which routes may attach to the created Gateway's listeners. Defaults to `Same`: a Gateway
this chart owns should not be attachable from another namespace unless that is asked for.
allowedRoutes.title: allowedRoutes

annotations.description: Annotations for the HTTPRoute and the created Gateway. Values may contain Go templates.
annotations.title: annotations

backendRefs.description:
Backends for rules that name none. Defaults to this chart's own Service. Weights are
honoured, so a traffic split needs no custom rule.
backendRefs.title: backendRefs

create.description:
Also create the Gateway itself. Leave off when the cluster already runs one — that is the
normal case, and one Gateway per application usually means one load balancer per
application. When on, a route that names no parent attaches to it automatically.
create.title: create

enabled.title: enabled

filters.description:
Filters applied to the default rule: `RequestHeaderModifier`, `ResponseHeaderModifier`,

gatewayClassName.description:

`nginx`. Required by `create`; a Gateway without one is never reconciled. Ignored otherwise.

Required unless `create` is set. A route with no hostnames matches every name its listener
accepts: on a Gateway this chart owns that is harmless, and sometimes the point — an install
reached by address has no DNS name to state. On a shared Gateway it means taking over traffic
meant for other applications, so the render refuses it.
hostnames.title: hostnames

parentRefs.description:
Gateways the route attaches to. Each entry takes `name` and optionally `namespace`,
`sectionName` (a single listener), `port`, `group` and `kind`; the API's defaults are filled
in. Values may contain Go templates.

A route that names no parent is accepted by the API server and then does nothing — no
listener ever programs it — so this is required unless `create` is set.
Example:
```yaml
parentRefs:
  - name: shared-gateway
    namespace: gateway-system
    sectionName: https
```
parentRefs.title: parentRefs

rules.description:

only narrows the path does not have to restate where the traffic goes.

Left empty, the route gets one rule matching `path` as a prefix — the Gateway API equivalent
of a single-path Ingress, and a complete configuration together with `hostnames`.

when `rules` is set.

convention by which one is looked up from the hostname. A ref naming another namespace
additionally needs a `ReferenceGrant` there, which this chart deliberately does not create
— a grant is the target namespace owner's to give.

networkPolicy.description:
Network policy configuration.

Every generated egress rule is scoped by a `to:` selector. An egress rule that lists only
ports is not a restriction — the NetworkPolicy API reads a missing `to` as "any
destination", so such a policy permits traffic to every in-cluster service and to the
cloud metadata endpoint.

cilium.description:
Cilium-only additions, used when `engine` is `cilium` or `both`. Everything above is
translated into the CiliumNetworkPolicy automatically; these are the rules the portable API
has no way to express.

`extraIngress`, `extraEgress` and the per-section `customRules` above are *not* carried over:
those are verbatim `networking.k8s.io/v1` rule objects and are not valid CNP. The fields
below are their counterparts.

description.description:
`spec.description`, which Cilium surfaces in `cilium policy get` and in Hubble flow
verdicts. The one place to record *why* a rule exists where an operator debugging a drop
will actually see it.
description.title: description

customRules.description: Additional egress rules in CiliumNetworkPolicy form, appended verbatim.
customRules.title: customRules

dnsMatchPatterns.description:
What the DNS proxy may resolve, e.g. `- matchPattern: "*.example.com"`. Defaults to
everything, which only permits the lookup — an answer is still only reachable if some
rule allows the address.
dnsMatchPatterns.title: dnsMatchPatterns

entityPorts.description: Restrict the `toEntities` rule to specific ports. Empty means all ports.
entityPorts.title: entityPorts

fqdnPorts.description: Ports the `toFQDNs` rule allows. Defaults to TCP/443.
fqdnPorts.title: fqdnPorts

httpRules.description:
L7 HTTP rules layered onto the `toFQDNs` rule, e.g.
`- method: GET` / `path: "/v1/.*"`. Turns "may reach this host" into "may make these
requests to this host". Costs a proxy hop per connection.
httpRules.title: httpRules

toEntities.description:
Named destination sets, e.g. `world` for everything outside the cluster, or
`kube-apiserver`. Not a synonym for the `egress.cidr`/`except` translation: `world` does
not carve out the cloud metadata endpoint the way those defaults do.
toEntities.title: toEntities

toFQDNs.description:
Destinations by name rather than by address, e.g. `- matchName: api.example.com` or
`- matchPattern: "*.example.com"`. This is the rule the CIDR-based `egress.https` was
always a poor approximation of: "may reach the internet on 443" permits every public host
that exists, where this permits the ones the application actually talks to.

Enforced against the addresses Cilium's DNS proxy saw returned for the name, so
`egress.dns.enabled` must stay on — the render fails if it is not.
toFQDNs.title: toFQDNs

enableDefaultDeny.description:
State default-deny explicitly rather than relying on it being implied by the presence of
rules. This is what makes the intentional default-deny case — a policy with an empty rule
list — actually deny, instead of being treated as no policy at all. Requires Cilium 1.16+.
enableDefaultDeny.title: enableDefaultDeny

for the window in which a cluster is migrating between CNIs.

The engine picks the dialect, not the rules — every value below is translated either way, so
switching is a one-line change. `both` is additive rather than stricter: policies selecting
one pod union their allowances, so it is a migration setting and not a hardening one.

dashboards there is only one carrier — `PrometheusRule` is already the operator's own CRD — and
no per-object cross-namespace grant: which namespaces a Prometheus loads rules from is decided

in a Go template, the rule files mark every selector with an always-true placeholder matcher
and the library swaps it for a real one — see the note in `_prometheus.tpl`. Consuming charts
normally derive `matcher` rather than exposing it raw.

prometheusRule.description: The PrometheusRule carrying this chart's alerting and recording rules.

additionalRuleGroups.description:
Extra rule groups, appended to the ones this chart ships. Each entry is a Prometheus rule
group — a `name`, a list of `rules`, optionally an `interval` — emitted as written: they are
not passed through Helm's template engine, so a `$labels` reference in an annotation reaches
Prometheus intact instead of being resolved to an empty string on the way past. That also
means no `{{ .Release.Name }}` in them.

`additionalRuleLabels` does reach these, because it describes the release rather than the
rules — skipping them would route exactly the alerts you wrote yourself back into the
rotation you were keeping this install out of. Precedence flips: a label you set on your own
rule wins, since it is already you speaking rather than a default of the chart's.

This is what makes `disabledAlerts` honest: switch a shipped rule off and write your own
with the arithmetic you wanted. A group whose name collides with a shipped one is refused,
because Prometheus rejects the whole object rather than the duplicate.
additionalRuleGroups.title: additionalRuleGroups

additionalRuleLabels.description:
Labels merged into every alert this chart ships, for Alertmanager routing. This is how a
test server keeps itself out of the on-call rotation. Applied to alerting rules only: a
label on a recording rule changes the identity of the series it records, and every
dashboard panel and expression reading it would silently stop matching.

These beat the labels in the rule files, which is the point of them, and lose to
`severityOverrides`, which is more specific.

Example: `{team: platform, tier: staging}`
additionalRuleLabels.title: additionalRuleLabels

disabledAlerts.description:
Alerts to drop, by name. Refused when the name is not one this chart ships — a typo here
is the one failure the whole feature must not produce, because it leaves the values file
saying an alert is off while it still pages. The rules stay in `rules/` and stay tested;
only the rendered object loses them.

Example: `[TeamSpeakServerRestarted]`
disabledAlerts.title: disabledAlerts

disabledGroups.description:
Rule groups to drop entirely, by name. Refused when the name is not one this chart
ships, and refused for a group holding recording rules: the alerts and the dashboard read
the series those produce, so dropping one leaves panels blank and expressions matching
nothing, and neither reports an error. Use `disabledAlerts` for the alerts instead.

Example: `[teamspeak-capacity]`
disabledGroups.title: disabledGroups

enabled.description: Create the PrometheusRule. Requires the Prometheus Operator CRDs.
enabled.title: enabled

forOverrides.description:
Per-alert `for` duration, keyed by alert name — how long the condition must hold before
the alert fires. A Prometheus duration such as `30s`, `15m` or `1h30m`; write zero as `0m`
so YAML keeps it a string. Anything Prometheus cannot parse is refused here, because it
would otherwise be refused at load time and take the alert's whole rule group down with it.

Example: `{TeamSpeakExporterDown: 5m}`
forOverrides.title: forOverrides

labels.description:
Extra labels for the PrometheusRule, e.g. the `release` label a Prometheus Operator
instance selects rules on. Without the one your instance selects, the object is created
and never loaded.
labels.title: labels

namespace.description:
Namespace for the PrometheusRule. Empty uses the release namespace. A Prometheus loads
rules from whichever namespaces its `ruleNamespaceSelector` names, which this chart cannot
reach; landing the object in one of them is the move that is left. The rules stay scoped to
this release either way — `scope` is derived from the release, not from where the object
lands.
namespace.title: namespace

scope.description:
How far the rules are scoped. A PrometheusRule is not confined to its own namespace, so
`none` makes this release alert on every other TeamSpeak in the cluster as well.
`namespace` rewrites every selector to match only this release's namespace; `release`
narrows that further to this release's own pods, which is what you want when two TeamSpeak
servers share a namespace.
scope.title: scope

severityOverrides.description:
Per-alert `severity` label, keyed by alert name. The most specific setting there is, so
it beats both the rule file and `additionalRuleLabels`. Refused for an alert this chart
does not ship, and for one the same values disable.

Example: `{TeamSpeakSlotsNearlyFull: critical}`
severityOverrides.title: severityOverrides

thresholds.description:
Threshold overrides, keyed by alert name and then by tunable name. Only the thresholds
this chart declares in [`rules/tunables.yaml`](rules/tunables.yaml) can be moved, and that
file says what each one means and what it is bounded by; setting anything else is refused
with the list of names that would have worked.

Not every number in a rule is a threshold somebody chose. `TeamSpeakExporterDown` and
`TeamSpeakServerOffline` compare against zero, which is structural rather than a judgement,
so neither is offered here. Disable the alert and re-add your own through
`additionalRuleGroups` if you need different arithmetic.

Example: `{TeamSpeakSlotsNearlyFull: {ratio: 0.8}}`
thresholds.title: thresholds

cilium.description:
Cilium-only additions, used when `engine` is `cilium` or `both`. Every rule above is
translated automatically; these are the ones the portable API has no way to express.

`extraIngress`, `extraEgress` and the per-section `customRules` above are *not* carried over:
those are verbatim `networking.k8s.io/v1` rule objects and are not valid CNP. The fields
below are their counterparts.

description.description:
`spec.description`, which Cilium surfaces in `cilium policy get` and in Hubble flow
verdicts. The one place to record why a rule exists where an operator debugging a dropped
voice packet will actually see it.

accountingFQDNs.description:
The licensing endpoint by name, replacing the internet-wide CIDR rule for
`egress.accounting`. This is the rule the portable policy cannot state: the accounting
host's address changes over time, so `networking.k8s.io/v1` can only permit TCP/2008 to
the entire public internet.

Ships empty on purpose. A wrong hostname here does not fail loudly — it takes the
virtual server offline at the next licence check — so it is stated rather than guessed.
Example:
```yaml
accountingFQDNs:
  - matchName: accounting.teamspeak.com
```
accountingFQDNs.title: accountingFQDNs

customRules.title: customRules

dnsMatchPatterns.description:
What the DNS proxy may resolve, e.g. `- matchPattern: "*.teamspeak.com"`. Defaults to

dnsMatchPatterns.title: dnsMatchPatterns

toEntities.title: toEntities

weblistFQDNs.description:
The public server list by name, replacing the internet-wide CIDR rule for
`egress.weblist`. Same reasoning, and the same reason it ships empty.
weblistFQDNs.title: weblistFQDNs
